lead: A flow net is a mesh of two line families. Streamlines show the direction of flow, and equipotential lines join points of equal velocity potential. In a two-dimensional irrotational flow the two families cross at right angles, and the mesh cells are drawn as curvilinear squares. The mesh turns a hard field problem into a sketch: line spacing gives speed, and the number of channels gives discharge per unit depth. Engineers use flow nets to estimate flow past a body, flow through a contraction in a wide channel, and seepage under a dam.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.7 for the stream function ψ and velocity potential φ, and Chapter 2.3 for streamlines.

blocks.text: A streamline is a curve whose tangent at every point is the velocity direction. Along one streamline the stream function ψ is constant. The stream function exists for any two-dimensional incompressible flow, as Chapter 2.7 explains. An equipotential line joins points with the same velocity potential φ. The velocity potential exists only when the flow is irrotational. In many flow-net problems the flow is both incompressible and irrotational, so both families exist.

At a point, velocity is tangent to the streamline and normal to the equipotential line. Those two directions are at right angles. Therefore streamlines and equipotential lines meet at 90°. This right-angle rule is the main check on a hand-drawn net. If a crossing is not square, the sketch is wrong.

blocks.where: v is the speed in m/s; Δψ is the change in stream function between two neighbouring streamlines, in m²/s; Δn is the perpendicular distance between them, in m.

blocks.text: For the potential lines, v = Δφ / Δs, where Δφ is the change in velocity potential and Δs is the distance between neighbouring equipotential lines. In a curvilinear square Δn ≈ Δs, so the changes in ψ and φ across one cell have the same size.

Start from the boundaries. A solid wall is a streamline because no fluid crosses it. A reservoir face is an equipotential because the total head is constant along it. Fix these lines before drawing any interior line.

items: Draw the boundaries: solid walls as streamlines, reservoir faces as equipotentials.
Choose one increment and use it for both families: Δψ = Δφ.
Sketch streamlines at equal steps of ψ and equipotentials at equal steps of φ with that same increment.

Adjust the net by adding or removing whole streamlines and whole equipotentials, which changes the increments together, until every cell is a curvilinear square: the average distance between streamlines equals the average distance between equipotentials.
Count the flow channels N_f and the potential drops N_d.

blocks.text: The cells need not be perfect squares. A curvilinear square has four right-angle corners and an average width equal to its average length. In a narrow passage the cells become small, which correctly shows fast flow. Iterate: moving one line changes the neighbouring cells, so redraw until the square condition holds everywhere.

blocks.where: q is the discharge per unit depth in m²/s (equivalently m³/s per metre of depth); N_f is the number of flow channels between the two boundary streamlines; Δψ is the change in stream function between neighbouring streamlines in m²/s.

blocks.text: Between two neighbouring streamlines the discharge per unit depth is Δψ. With N_f channels between the two boundary streamlines, q = N_f Δψ. The unit is square metres per second (equivalently cubic metres per second per metre of depth). This is the flow rate through a slice one metre thick. Count channels as spaces between streamlines, not the streamlines themselves.

Velocity at a point is inversely proportional to the spacing between streamlines. Close lines mean a small Δn and a large v. This is why the net crowds near a sharp corner or a sudden contraction. The same crowding appears between equipotential lines.

blocks.where: Δh is the head drop between neighbouring equipotential lines in m; H is the total head difference between the two boundary equipotentials in m; N_d is the number of equipotential divisions.

blocks.text: Uses include sketching flow past a cylinder or an airfoil, flow through a sudden contraction in a wide rectangular channel or duct (a pipe contraction is axisymmetric and needs its own treatment), and seepage under a dam. In seepage, the net gives flow rate and pore pressure; a soil mechanics course takes that calculation further. Some syllabi call φ lines equipotential lines and ask only for the number of flow channels and potential drops.

figure.caption: The sketch is adjusted until every cell is a curvilinear square; then the number of flow channels gives the discharge. Notice that boundaries are fixed before any interior line is drawn.

examples.question: In a flow net, the stream function changes by 0.05 m²/s between neighbouring streamlines. There are 10 flow channels between the two boundary streamlines, and 20 equipotential divisions for a total head difference of 2 m. Find (a) the discharge per unit depth between the boundary streamlines and (b) the head drop between neighbouring equipotential lines.
steps: Write the data: Δψ = 0.05 m²/s, N_f = 10, N_d = 20, H = 2 m.
Discharge per unit depth: q = N_f Δψ = 10 × 0.05 = 0.5 m²/s (that is 0.5 m³/s through each 1 m thick slice).
Head drop per equipotential division: Δh = H / N_d = 2 / 20 = 0.1 m.
examples.answer: The discharge is 0.5 m²/s (0.5 m³/s per metre of depth), and the head drop between neighbouring equipotential lines is 0.1 m.
examples.check:
delta_psi = 0.05
Nf = 10
Nd = 20
H = 2.0
q = Nf * delta_psi
dh = H / Nd
print(q)
print(dh)

traps: Drawing rectangular cells instead of curvilinear squares. The square condition is average width equals average length, with right-angle corners.
Counting the boundary streamlines as flow channels. N_f is the number of spaces between streamlines, not the number of streamlines.
Treating the head drop per equipotential division as a velocity. Δh is in metres of head, not m/s.
Confusing ψ and φ increments. Δψ gives discharge between streamlines; Δφ gives velocity through v = Δφ / Δs, and only for irrotational flow.
Forgetting that q is per unit depth. A two-dimensional flow net gives q in m²/s, which is the flow rate through a slice one metre thick.

quiz.q: What does each family of lines in a flow net represent?
quiz.a: Streamlines show the flow direction and are lines of constant stream function ψ. Equipotential lines join points of constant velocity potential φ.

quiz.q: Why do streamlines and equipotentials cross at 90°?
quiz.a: Velocity is tangent to a streamline and normal to an equipotential line. The two directions are perpendicular, so the lines cross at 90°.

quiz.q: A net has Δψ = 0.02 m²/s between neighbouring streamlines and 8 flow channels. Find q, the discharge per unit depth.
quiz.a: q = N_f Δψ = 8 × 0.02 = 0.16 m²/s (0.16 m³/s per metre of depth).

quiz.q: A flow net has a total head difference of 3.0 m and 15 equal potential drops. Find the head drop between neighbouring equipotential lines.
A student draws cells that are long and thin near a wall. What is wrong, and what should be changed?
quiz.a: The curvilinear-square condition is not met because average length and width differ. Adjust the neighbouring streamline or equipotential spacing until the average cell dimensions are equal, keeping right angles.

quiz.q: Why is a solid wall a streamline and a reservoir face an equipotential?
quiz.a: No flow crosses a solid wall, so the wall is tangent to velocity and is a streamline. Along a reservoir face the total head is constant, so the velocity potential is constant and the face is an equipotential.

quiz.q: Two points lie in the same flow channel. At A the streamlines are 20 mm apart; at B they are 5 mm apart. Compare the speeds.
quiz.a: v ∝ 1/Δn, so v_B / v_A = 20 / 5 = 4. The speed at B is four times the speed at A.

beyond: Not for the exam. Potential-flow codes solve Laplace's equation on a grid instead of drawing a net. General-purpose CFD codes solve the full Navier–Stokes equations, but the same ψ and φ idea still sits inside them. Flow nets remain a quick field check for dam seepage, well fields and hydraulic structures. They also lead to conformal mapping, where a complex coordinate maps simple flow into a complicated shape. Search for potential flow, Laplace equation and conformal mapping.
